name: Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyradiculoneuropathy

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) Guillain-Barré Syndrome Criteria

criteria.description: Progressive weakness of more than one limb
Areflexia or hyporeflexia in affected limbs
Elevated cerebrospinal fluid protein with normal white cell count (cytoalbuminologic dissociation)
Electrophysiological evidence of demyelination on nerve conduction studies

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Progressive weakness of more than one limb with areflexia or hyporeflexia; supportive findings such as CSF cytoalbuminologic dissociation or demyelinating features on nerve conduction studies strengthen diagnosis.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is clinical but supported by CSF and electrophysiological studies; exclusion of mimics is essential.

laboratory: Elevated CSF protein with normal white cell count (cytoalbuminologic dissociation)
Normal or mildly elevated inflammatory markers
imaging: MRI spine may show nerve root enhancement
other: Nerve conduction studies showing demyelination (prolonged distal latencies, conduction block, slowed conduction velocities)

distinguishingFeatures: Chronic progressive or relapsing course rather than acute
Predominantly motor involvement without sensory symptoms
Axonal rather than demyelinating features on nerve conduction studies
More common in certain geographic regions (e.g., Asia)

redFlags: Rapid progression of weakness within hours
Severe autonomic instability (e.g., arrhythmias, blood pressure crises)
references: Hughes RA, Cornblath DR. Guillain-Barré syndrome. Lancet. 2005 Nov 5;366(9497):1653-66.
National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke. Guillain-Barré Syndrome Fact Sheet.
